newsitem.title: USA: Study finds cholesterol drug can cut stroke risk.
newsitem.headline: Study finds cholesterol drug can cut stroke risk.

text.p: The newest class of cholesterol-lowering drugs have the added benefit of reducing stroke risk by up to 30 percent in patients with heart disease, researchers at the Bowman Gray/Baptist Hospital Medical Center said.
Dr. John Crouse III, the study's primary author, said the study found that cholesterol-lowering drugs work on all of the body's blood vessels.
Crouse and his colleagues analyzed the data from 12 clinical trials that looked at the relationship between heart attacks and reductase inhibitors, a group of cholesterol lowering drugs.

The analysis, which was presented to the American Heart Association meeting, showed the drugs, such as Bristol-Myers Squibb Co's Pravachol (Pravastatin), Sandoz AG's Lescol (Lovastatin), and Merck & Co Inc's Zocor (Simvastatin), reduced strokes by 30 percent in patients with heart disease.
In patients without heart disease, the risk of stroke was cut by 14 percent, the study said.
The researchers theorize that the reduction in strokes is associated with the drugs' ability to slow down disease of the neck arteries and to reduce heart attack risk, the study said.
Another theory about how the drugs might prevent strokes is that they improve arterial function, the study said.
